__FUND_COUNT__ funds · round-level evidence

Who funded what in crypto, one round at a time

Every investment here exists because a fund appeared in a funding round, not because it put itself on a portfolio page. The dataset was built in one pass over every project page on the source, then inverted to fund. That ordering is the whole point: fund pages show ten rows and quietly drop the failures.

01

Fund pages measure survivors, so the round is the unit

Two measured properties disqualify fund pages as a primary source. First, a display limit: the source's fund page renders a fixed handful of rounds, and pagination redirects back to page one. Second, survivorship bias: a fund maintaining its own portfolio page has no reason to keep written-off companies listed.

Both effects point the same way — scraping per fund measures the winners and calls it a portfolio. So this dataset reads every project page instead, parses all investors per round, and only then inverts the index to fund.

Portfolio size is the easiest metric to score well on and says the least. Lead rate is the more honest number: it is independent of how many rounds a fund joined. Click any card to filter the explorer below to that fund.

04

Rank pairs by shared rounds and you rank portfolio size

So every figure below is scored against a permutation null that holds two things fixed: each fund keeps its own number of rounds, and each round keeps its own number of these __FUND_COUNT__ funds. Swaps stay inside a calendar year, so a fund's active window is preserved too. Lift is what actually happened divided by what that null expects — 1.0 is exactly chance.

The biggest pairings, against what chance expected of them

The twelve most frequent pairings, each drawn from what the null expected to what was observed. A marker to the right of its expected point means the pair beat chance; to the left means it fell short despite the volume. Note how small the gaps are — these pairs are frequent mainly because both funds are busy.

How often each fund is the only one of the __FUND_COUNT__ in a round

A high bar means the fund rarely shares a cap table with the others in this set. That is a statement about this sample, not about whether the fund co-invests at all — it may well share rounds with hundreds of funds outside this set.
